output.why:
Letter A has the strongest ending of the six: "Each year at dinner he told me my watch ran fast. It did." It turns the whole mechanism of the crime into one quiet fact about a man's habit, and it does this without a summary. Its voice is civil, self-regarding, and believable, and the clockwork is clear: the fast watch, the reset regulator, the one admitted lie, and the house keeping its own time. The line "A house of this kind keeps its own time" edges toward a moral, which is the only flaw.

Letter C is the most restrained of the six. It keeps the physical detail concrete (the Op. 9 nocturne chosen for its volume, the watch fast by two minutes and "in your waistcoat", the wages to Rosa) and never explains the mechanism. "In thirty years she has never once asked me where I have been" does more for Odile than any direct statement. Its ending, "I have no more to add", is flat, but the flatness suits the voice. It sits just below A because A's last line lands harder.

Letter F has a strong, believable voice and a good quiet ending ("I shall not need to be fetched"). The repeater Aurèle spent four years on, and "a repeater cannot be made to unsay what it has said", are fine images. It loses ground to epigram: "In La Chaux-de-Fonds time is something one agrees about" and "I am troubled by its grammar now" are the writer showing off.

Letter B is vivid in places ("The room was full of that sound, and then it was not"; "I will not describe the rest"), but it over-instructs ("Please see that they are told nothing they have not earned") and closes on a Latin tag that the letter has not earned. Its ending is the weakest part.

Letter D has a good ledger voice ("I have always preferred a history to an opinion"; "it was the worst of it"). But the timestamps (22:33, 22:35, 22:38) make the clockwork explicit and mechanical, and the explanation of what the confessor failed to reckon with reads as an inventory rather than a confession.

Letter E is the most explanatory. It announces its own confession, spells out the reason for Félix and the letter's contents, and includes clumsy lines ("so, I think, was Félix's brandy in the library"). Its best line, "I have not been a careful liar. I have been a careful physician", is undercut by the surrounding over-explanation. Its ending is the least controlled of the six.
